summary:
Denmark has permitted legal gender recognition by self-declaration since 1 September 2014. The procedure requires a stated request and a six-month reflection period, with no medical evaluation or psychiatric diagnosis, and it was the first system of its kind in Europe. Danish passports are issued with an 'X' sex descriptor, so a non-binary visitor or resident can hold a document that does not assert a binary marker.

Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is prohibited. The Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment and services. The 1996 Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market named sexual orientation but did not name gender identity or expression; a 2015 court ruling in a case brought by a trans woman against her former employer held that gender identity and expression fall within the Act. The F&M Global Barometers profile records that workplace anti-discrimination law has covered gender identity since 2015 and that fair-housing protection on gender-identity grounds has been in place throughout 2011 to 2024.

Hate crime penalties added by 2004 amendments to the Penal Code apply to crimes motivated by sexual orientation; the sourced account does not extend that enumeration to gender identity, leaving the coverage of gender-motivated offences a separate question from the anti-discrimination provisions.

In custody, the leading Danish authority is a Supreme Court ruling of 10 September 2024 holding that it is not a human-rights violation for a trans inmate to serve in a men's prison department. Visitors and residents facing detention should expect placement on the basis of assigned sex rather than legal or lived gender.

Access to transition-related healthcare is not purely self-determined despite the self-declaration rule for documents. Patients seeking hormone therapy report being required to present in ways reflecting stereotypical gender roles, for example trans men being asked to give 'male' answers in clinical settings. This gatekeeping rests on patient reports rather than on a codified policy.

Violence risk is documented. In July 2024 a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen. The UN Committee Against Torture, in its eighth periodic review, found that some trans people, some QTIBIPOC people and some migrants report denial of access to spaces and services, and threats; the committee urged psychosocial counselling provision and remedy for intersex people. Anti-trans discourse intensified while parliament debated lowering the legal gender recognition age limit, and the outcome of that debate is not established in the sources.

Asylum practice has recognised gender identity persecution. In February 2013 a Guatemalan trans woman, Fernanda Milan, became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark, citing police attacks and threats tied to her trans activism as grounds for refusal of return.
tangentialFactors:
Denmark is consistently ranked among the world's better jurisdictions for LGBTQ+ rights, and activists attribute the comparatively low temperature of its trans debate to the self-ID law. It was the first country to recognise same-sex partnerships, in 1989, and same-sex marriage followed in 2012; same-sex couples may also adopt.

No ban on conversion therapy is in force. A bill to prohibit the practice was revived in August 2026 and its passage is unresolved in the sources.

In August 2024 the government announced a plan to strengthen recognition of multi-parent families of three or four parents, an area of family law adjacent to but distinct from partner recognition.

Denmark signed a UN resolution against discrimination based on sex characteristics in March 2025, a position statement rather than a domestic remedy for intersex people.
localsOnly:
Discrimination reporting is substantial. The Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT+ barometer records that 38% of homosexual and bisexual respondents report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance, and that hate speech targeting sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics recurs annually.

Workplace conditions are comparatively open. A 2019 report found 69% of LGBT respondents were open about their sexual orientation to colleagues, while 9% felt they could not be.

Health outcomes among young people are weak relative to the general population: 40% of LGBTI students aged 15 to 25 reported self-harm in the preceding year, a rate two to three times that of their classmates.

The F&M Global Barometers profile records that freedom from arbitrary arrest on the basis of gender identity has been affirmed in every year from 2011 to 2024. The UN Committee Against Torture's review recommended expansion of psychosocial counselling and a remedy for intersex people, neither of which the sources confirm as implemented.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not establish whether the 2004 Penal Code hate crime penalties extend to offences motivated by gender identity or expression; they name sexual orientation only. Whether hate-crime charging practice in fact covers gender-motivated offences is unresolved here.

The outcome of the parliamentary debate on lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition is not established in the sources, and no current minimum age figure is sourced.

The hormone therapy gatekeeping described rests on patient accounts collected by a Wikipedia country profile rather than on published clinical protocol; the existence of a formal rule cannot be confirmed from the inventory.

The conversion therapy bill revived in August 2026 has no confirmed legislative status beyond the revival.

The Supreme Court's 2024 ruling addresses a trans inmate placed in a men's department; the sources do not state how the placement question is handled for trans women in other custodial settings.
